qt: to the Commission Tom Berendsen (PPE), Jeroen Lenaers (PPE) Subject:

In October, the Commission launched an anti-subsidy investigation into electric vehicles from China on the European market. In December, it became clear that Chinese company BYD wants to open an electric car manufacturing plant in Hungary. Reports this week1 suggest that Hungary will spend some EUR 240 million of EU money from the REPowerEU fund to support BYD in Hungary. The purpose of this money is precisely to make the European Union less dependent on countries like China. By supporting BYD, Hungary is directly weakening the competitive position of European companies, undermining the EU’s goals of strengthening our strategic autonomy. 1.
Does the Commission agree with us that Hungary’s support to BYD through allocated REPowerEU funds runs counter to the Union’s objective of strengthening our strategic autonomy?
Is the Commission prepared to recover these funds?

What action will the Commission take to ensure that any measures resulting from the antisubsidy investigation into electric vehicles from China cannot be circumvented by companies such as BYD by moving some or all of their production to the European Union?
at: (English version) to the Commission Tom Berendsen (PPE), Jeroen Lenaers (PPE) (31 January 2024) Subject: Hungarian aid to Chinese carmaker threatens European competitiveness In October, the Commission launched an anti-subsidy investigation into electric vehicles from China on the European market. In December, it became clear that Chinese company BYD wants to open an electric car manufacturing plant in Hungary. Reports this week (1) suggest that Hungary will spend some EUR 240 million of EU money from the REPowerEU fund to support BYD in Hungary. The purpose of this money is precisely to make the European Union less dependent on countries like China. By supporting BYD, Hungary is directly weakening the competitive position of European companies, undermining the EU’s goals of strengthening our strategic autonomy. 1. Does the Commission agree with us that Hungary’s support to BYD through allocated REPowerEU funds runs counter to the Union’s objective of strengthening our strategic autonomy? 2.
Is the Commission prepared to recover these funds?

3. What action will the Commission take to ensure that any measures resulting from the anti-subsidy investigation into electric vehicles from China cannot be circumvented by companies such as BYD by moving some or all of their production to the European Union? (15 April 2024) In the Hungarian Recovery and Resilience Plan (RRP) two investments support the purchase of electric vehicles (EVs) by businesses and one promotes the installation of recharging points. These will be financed by loans from the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) (2) up to EUR 240 million. Pursuing the objectives of REPowerEU, similarly to measures of other Member States, these aim to boost sustainable mobility. The recipient companies can choose the EVs to be purchased under the related measures. The measures are to be implemented in a way that no particular economic operator would unduly benefit from them. The annex (3) to the Council Implementing Decision on the approval of the revised RRP specifies that investment decisions must be taken in a transparent, independent and market-conform way. The Commission will verify the fulfilment of milestones and targets as part of upcoming RRF payment requests. For Hungary, no disbursement is possible until it has satisfactorily implemented the 27 ‘super milestones’ related to the protection of EU financial interests. As with all investments under the RRF, it is the Member State’s responsibility to properly implement its RRP in line with EU and national rules, including state aid rules. In the event of undue actions from third countries, there are also dedicated instruments — outside the RRF’s remit — that may be used, even if investments are supported by the RRF, such as trade defence instruments, the EU Foreign Direct Investment Screening Regulation (4) or the EU Foreign Subsidies Regulation (5). It is premature to conclude on the ongoing anti-subsidy investigation on imports of EVs from China. However, in general, EU trade defence instruments include tools to address the circumvention of any measures imposed.
